Abstract 18

Prospective influenza A (IAV) RNA monitoring at 190 wastewater treatment plants across the 19

US identified increases in IAV RNA concentrations at 59 plants in spring 2024, after the typical 20

seasonal influenza period, coincident with the identification of highly pathogenic avian influenza 21

(subtype H5N1) circulating in dairy cattle in the US. We developed and validated a hydrolysis- 22

probe RT-PCR assay for quantification of the H5 hemagglutinin gene. We applied it 23

retrospectively to samples from three plants where springtime increases were identified. The H5 24

marker was detected at all three plants coinciding with the increases. Plants were located in a 25

state with confirmed outbreaks of highly pathogenic avian influenza, H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b, in 26

dairy cattle. Concentrations of the H5 gene approached overall influenza A virus gene 27

concentrations, suggesting a large fraction of IAV inputs were H5 subtypes. At two of the 28

wastewater plants, industrial discharges containing animal waste, including milk byproducts, 29

were permitted to discharge into sewers. Our findings demonstrate wastewater monitoring can 30

detect animal-associated influenza contributions, and highlight the need to consider industrial 31

and agricultural inputs into wastewater. This work illustrates wastewater monitoring’s value for 32

comprehensive influenza surveillance for diseases with zoonotic potential across human and 33

animal populations. 34

Introduction 37

Respiratory infections are the fourth largest cause of death worldwide1–3. Among these, 38

influenza viruses are one of the most common causes of viral epidemics of respiratory 39

infection, with an estimated one billion cases each year4. In recent years, a majority of 40

these influenza infections have been caused by Influenza A virus (IAV)5, which has 41

been responsible for all global epidemics of influenza. Influenza A viruses are found in 42

both humans and animals; H5N1 influenza is a highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) 43

that emerged in the late 1990s and has become widespread in wild birds and has 44

zoonotic potential. A new H5N1 clade (2.3.4.4b) has caused widespread outbreaks 45

since 20226. Tens of millions of chickens have been culled in the US to control 46

outbreaks, and there is a threat of zoonotic transmission to humans. In 2024 this 47

outbreak spread to dairy cattle and was associated with one known human case, the 48

second case of HPAI documented in the United States6. 49

50

Wastewater surveillance of influenza A has been implemented across the United 51

States, and concentrations of viral RNA in wastewater have been shown to align with 52

clinical surveillance metrics including influenza-like illness, influenza hospitalizations, 53

and deaths.7–10 As a result, it is becoming a routine public health tool for influenza 54

outbreaks and provides low-cost, real-time, population level data on influenza 55

outbreaks, particularly in locations with limited clinical testing11. The utility of these data 56

and responses are predicated on the assumption that the majority of the contributions to 57

these measurements are from human sources, rather than influenzas with zoonotic 58

potential such as H5N1 and H7N912,13. Recent increases in the spread of HPAI to new 59

species, particularly subtype H5N1 clade 2.3. 4.4b spread in dairy cattle6, have raised 60

questions about wastewater contributions from avian and bovine sources14,15. 61

62

Studies have demonstrated the potential for subtyping circulating IAV directly from 63

wastewater samples7,16. IAV subtypes are differentiated by two main surface 64

glycoproteins, hemagglutinin (HA) and the neuraminidase (NA)17. We previously applied 65

hydrolysis probe-based RT-PCR assays for H1, H3, N1, and N2 to wastewater to 66

identify circulating IAV subtypes. However, to date, a hydrolysis probe-based RT-PCR 67

assay for the H5 marker in IAV has not been applied to wastewater. 68

69

In this study, we use prospective measurements of IAV M gene, which detects all IAV 70

subtypes, in wastewater solids from 190 wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) to 71

identify WWTP showing springtime increases in IAV concentrations after the typical 72

influenza season ends, coincident with the identification and spread of HPAI in animal 73

populations in the US. We developed a novel RT-PCR hydrolysis-probe assay to detect 74

the H5 subtype of IAV. After assay validation, we applied it to samples to measure 75

Methods 78

H5 assay design. Influenza A H5 subtype genome sequences were downloaded from 79

the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) in Feb 2023 and 80

supplemented with additional newer sequences available from NCBI and GISAID in 81

April 2024. Sequences were aligned, and primers and probes were designed to target 82

the hemagglutinin (HA) gene using Primer3Plus. Parameters used in assay 83

development (eg, sequence length and GC content) are provided elsewhere10. The 84

forward primer is: TATAGARGGAGGATGGCAGG, reverse primer: 85

ACDGCCTCAAAYTGAGTGTT, and probe: AGGGGAGTGGKTACGCTGCRGAC (also 86

in Table S1, Figure S1).  The primers and probes were confirmed to be specific and 87

sensitive for influenza A containing the H5 subtype of the HA gene in silico using NCBI 88

BLAST. 89

90

The assay was tested in vitro against nucleic acids from a large collection of respiratory 91

pathogens (Table S2) including non-H5 influenza subtypes. When panels were 92

composed of whole viruses or bacteria, their nucleic-acids were extracted and purified 93

as described below for the wastewater solids samples and then used neat as template 94

in droplet digital RT-PCR assays. Assays were run in a single well using the cycling 95

conditions and post processing using a droplet reader as described below for the 96

wastewater samples in singleplex. Synthetic nucleic acid gene blocks purchased from 97

IDT (Coralville, Iowa) were used as a positive control for the H5 marker. 98

99

Prospective IAV M gene testing in wastewater. Wastewater samples were obtained 100

from 190 wastewater treatment plants located in 41 states for a prospective wastewater 101

monitoring project. Samples are collected 3 to 7 times per week between 7/1/23 and 102

4/22/24 (month/day/year format, n=19,323). Samples are shipped overnight to the 103

laboratory at 4°C where they were processed immediately.  During the time between 104

sample collection and transport (0-3 days), we expect minimal losses of the RNA target 105

based on results of IAV RNA persistence studies18. Upon receipt of the laboratory, 106

samples are processed immediately to measure IAV M gene and PMMoV gene 107

concentrations in the solid fraction of wastewater. Since the methods are described in 108

detail in several different publications8,19, they are not provided in detail here. PMMoV is 109

an endogenous plant virus present in wastewater and serves as an internal process 110

control. Briefly, solids are isolated from the samples, suspended in a buffer at a low 111

enough concentration so as to minimize inhibition19, and subjected to nucleic-acid 112

extraction and purification (Chemagic Viral DNA/RNA 300 Kit H96, PerkinElmer, 113

Shelton, CT), and inhibitor removal (Zymo OneStep PCR Inhibitor Removal Kit, Irvine, 114

neat as template in 6 to 10 replicate droplet digital RT-PCR reaction wells to measure 116

IAV and 1:100 diluted in 2 to 10 replicate wells to measure PMMoV. The process 117

includes negative and positive extraction and PCR controls, as well as a measure of 118

recovery as determined from spiking exogenous bovine coronavirus. The M gene target 119

is present in all subtypes of IAV including the H5N1 subtype and the current circulating 120

clade 2.3.4.4b. Concentrations are expressed as copies per gram dry weight. After 121

obtaining these measurements, nucleic acids are biobanked at -80°C. 122

123

Retrospective Influenza A M gene and H5 testing in wastewater. Biobanked 124

samples between February 4 and April 16, 2024 from two wastewater treatment plant 125

(WWTP) sites of the City of Amarillo Water Utilities Division in Texas (hereafter 126

described as the “North” and “South” sites in Potter/Randall County, TX), as well as a 127

WWTP in Dallas County, Texas were used to measure concentrations of H5 marker 128

(samples were biobanked for up to 2 months, Table S3 provides exact dates of samples 129

run, n=78 samples). The Potter/Randall County City of Amarillo plants provide 24-hour 130

composited influent samples and the Dallas County plant provides settled solids from 131

the primary clarifier. Plants service areas with separate sanitary sewer systems. The 132

South and North sites in Potter/Randall County and the Dallas County site serve 133

approximately 60,000, 140,000, and 186,000 people. Several industries are permitted to 134

discharge wastewater to both City of Amarillo Water Utilities Division sanitary sewer 135

systems including animal product processing facilities. 136

137

Concentrations of the H5 marker and the IAV M gene were measured in multiplex using 138

an AutoDG Automated Droplet Generator (Bio-Rad, Hercules, CA), Mastercycler Pro 139

(Eppendforf, Enfield, CT) thermocycler, and a QX600 Droplet Reader (Bio-Rad). The 140

IAV M gene was measured again in the biobanked samples to document potential RNA 141

degradation. In addition an assay for the N gene of SARS-CoV-2 was included (results 142

not provided herein). Primers and probes for all the assays were purchased from IDT 143

(Coralville, Iowa). The H5 probe contained the fluorescent molecule FAM and the IAV M 144

gene probe contained ROX; both probes also contained ZEN, a proprietary internal 145

quencher from IDT; and IBFQ, Iowa Black FQ. Each of the 6 replicate nucleic-acid 146

extractions obtained from each sample were run neat as template in their own RT-PCR 147

well to measure the RNA targets. The cycling conditions were as follows: reverse 148

transcription at 50 °C for 60 min, enzyme activation at 95 °C for 5 min, 40 cycles of 149

denaturation at 95 °C for 30 s and annealing and extension at 59 °C for 30 s, enzyme 150

deactivation at 98 °C for 10 min then an indefinite hold at 4 °C. The ramp rate for 151

temperature changes were set to 2 °C/second and the final hold at 4 °C was performed 152

for a minimum of 30 min to allow the droplets to stabilize. Droplets were analyzed using 153

the QX600 Droplet Reader (Bio-Rad). A well had to have over 10,000 droplets for 154

158

Results from replicate wells were merged for analysis. Concentrations of the targets are 159

presented as copies per gram dry weight. Dry weight was determined using an aliquot 160

of solids and drying in an oven19. For a sample to be scored as a positive, there had to 161

be at least 3 positive droplets. The lowest measurable concentration is approximately 162

1000 copies/g dry weight. Errors are reported as standard deviations on the 163

measurements as obtained from QX Manager Software (Bio-Rad, version 2.0). 164

165

Influenza clinical data. Data on influenza-related emergency department visits by 166

health district20 and statewide influenza positivity rates21 for Texas were obtained from 167

publicly available data from the Texas Department of State Health Services. 168

Potter/Randall County sites are within public health district 1, and the Dallas County site 169

is within public health district 2/3. 170

171

Data analysis. Across the 190 WWTPs in the prospective study, we identified onset 172

and offset of IAV wastewater events using a previously published logic16. In short, IAV 173

wastewater event onset occurred when all samples analyzed in the previous 14 days 174

had concentrations of the IAV M gene ≥ 2000 cp/g and offset when less than or equal to 175

50% of the samples collected in the previous 14 days had concentrations ≥ 2000 cp/g. 176

Using this approach, we identified WWTPs that showed a secondary onset of IAV 177

wastewater events after the typical seasonal wastewater event offset. We also visually 178

examined IAV/PMMoV concentrations at WWTPs to subjectively identify those with a 179

noticeable spike, or increasing trends in concentrations observed after February 2024 180

when it was established that H5N1 was circulating. 181

Results 182

Assay sensitivity and specificity and QA/QC. Both in silico and in vitro testing 183

indicated the H5 assay is 100% specific. In vitro tests returned non-detects for all non- 184

target pathogens, including other influenza subtypes. The sensitivity of the assay is 185

estimated to be 90% as 10% of the influenza A H5 subtype sequences in GISAID and 186

NCBI have single nucleotide polymorphisms in the primer and probe regions. The H5 187

assay detects the circulating H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b. 188

Results are reported following Environmental Microbiology Minimal Information22 190

(EMMI) guidelines (checklist available with all wastewater data at 191

https://purl.stanford.edu/tr782wk3364). All positive and negative controls were positive 192

and negative, respectively indicating no contamination. Nucleic-acid extraction 193

efficiency for samples passed the quality control threshold of being over 0.1 for bovine 194

coronavirus (median = 1.1, IQR = 0.8 - 1.5); recoveries greater than one are likely a 195

result of errors associated with the measurements. PMMoV was detected at high 196

concentrations in all samples (median of 3.3x108, IQR = 1.9x108-6.4x108 cp/g) providing 197

further support of efficient nucleic-acid extraction. We compared concentrations of IAV 198

M gene in samples measured without any storage (during prospective monitoring) to 199

those measured in the same biobanked samples; the median ratio of IAV M gene 200

concentrations in biobanked to fresh samples was 1.3 (interquartile range 1.0 - 1.7, 201

n=78) suggesting limited degradation of RNA during storage. 202

203

Springtime increases in IAV M gene concentrations in WWTPs across the US. 204

Using the prospectively measured IAV RNA concentrations, we found, using all data 205

available on 24 April, 2024, that 44 of the 190 WWTPs showed a secondary IAV onset 206

event after their seasonal IAV event offset (Table S4); these are located across 18 207

different states. There were 99 WWTPs for which the seasonal IAV wastewater event 208

had not offset by the end of the data series; their IAV concentrations were visually 209

examined for recent increases during March and April, and 15 locations (Table S3) were 210

identified. Those 15 locations spanned 8 states. Example data from plants with distinct 211

spring increases are shown in Figure S2. 212

213

H5 marker prevalence in wastewater samples. Given that increases in wastewater 214

appear to be coincident with the identification of avian influenza circulating in the nation 215

(Figure S2), we decided to investigate whether the H5 marker was present in samples 216

from three “sentinel” WWTPs located in Texas where H5N1 was identified in cows14 217

(Figure 1). We found that prior to early to mid-March (depending on the WWTP), the H5 218

marker was non-detect in the wastewater solids. Subsequently, as IAV M gene 219

increased at the WWTPs, H5 marker became detectable at similar concentrations to the 220

IAV M gene. When detected, H5 concentration ranged from 5847 to 2,158,821 (median 221

= 29,364) cp/g. The IAV M gene concentrations measured during this time period are 222

among the highest ever measured in wastewater (Figure S3). In samples where H5 was 223

detected,the median ratio to IAV M gene was 0.6 at all three plants (IQR at Duck Creek: 224

0.6-0.6, Hollywood Road:  0.2 - 0.7, River Road: 0.4 - 0.8)  During this time, influenza 225

surveillance in Texas showed declined trends in influenza-related emergency 226

department visits in the associated public health regions (Figure 2). 227

Discussion 250

H5 influenza RNA was readily detected in wastewater solids at sites with atypical 251

increases in influenza A M gene concentrations in March and April 2024 during a period 252

of a known H5N1 outbreak in the US. The presence of H5 in municipal wastewater 253

indicates that contributions into the wastewater system include excretions or byproducts 254

containing influenza viral RNA with an H5 subtype, but do not indicate the species that 255

may be shedding an H5 influenza. During March and April 2024, increases in IAV M 256

gene concentrations at these plants were not associated with increases in human 257

influenza activity, as documented by the emergency room influenza case data in Texas. 258

However, both the increases in M gene concentrations and H5 detection occurred 259

immediately prior to and during reported outbreaks of H5N1 in dairy cattle in the 260

region14. These results suggest that wastewater monitoring is a viable method of 261

monitoring certain animal pathogens, and can provide a leading edge of detection that 262

is of particular importance for diseases with zoonotic potential like HPAI. 263

264

Hypothesized sources of H5. H5N1 outbreaks in dairy cattle were reported on March 265

25, 2024 in the Texas panhandle23, which contains the Potter/Randall County area. 266

There was also a human case of H5N1 reported in Amarillo, TX, in an individual who 267

worked at a commercial dairy cattle farm and reported close proximity to dairy cows24. 268

As of April 25, 2024, no outbreaks have been reported within the vicinity of Sunnyvale, 269

TX. Although no H5N1 outbreaks have been reported within the sewersheds of the 270

WWTPs in this study, both City of Amarillo Water Utilities Division receive effluent from 271

industries handling animal bioproducts, including dairies that receive milk from across 272

the region and beef processing plants (personal communication from local staff). At 273

least one dairy processing site is also permitted within the Dallas County sewershed 274

area. Dairy cattle have been reported to shed H5N1, as well as other viruses, in milk in 275

high quantities25,26. During the current outbreak, H5N1 has been detected in both raw 276

and pasteurized milk, according to USDA27. Pasteurization is expected to inactivate the 277

virus, although it may still be detectable as non-infectious genetic material can persist 278

past pasteurization28. Regardless of whether milk or milk products entering the sewer 279

system have undergone pasteurization or pre-treatment before they are discharged, our 280

methods detect viral nucleic acids and their detection does not imply viability. 281

282

Given the outbreaks in dairy milking cattle in the region14, reports of H5N1 shedding in 283

cow milk and detection in milk products on the shelf, and animal industry contributions 284

into wastewater at the three utilities, we hypothesize that dairy processing discharge 285

into the sewage system is driving the detection of H5 identified in wastewater solids. It is 286

important to note that, even if true, this does not eliminate the possibility of contributions 287

from other animals, including humans. If dairy industry activities in these sewersheds 288

are a primary source of H5 in wastewater, this suggests that there are may be 289

292

Limitations. The assay used here detects H5 broadly, and as such is not specific to 293

H5N1 or HPAI, and may include other, low pathogenic H5 influenza viruses (although 294

these are not expected to be circulating in these areas at this time29). HPAI genomes 295

contain one copy each of M and HA genes, so results of the assays should be 296

comparable, barring potential variability in assay performance and measurement errors. 297

Caution should be taken in interpreting these results for characterizing the current H5N1 298

outbreak; without isolating possible sources in the sewer network of the H5 299

contributions our hypotheses about the source of the signal cannot be fully 300

substantiated. However, multiple lines of evidence suggest animal sources. 301

302

This work shows that wastewater monitoring can provide an early warning for outbreaks 303

likely to produce contributions to the sewershed outside of the expected human- 304

associated inputs, including for animal outbreaks of diseases with zoonotic potential. In 305

Potter/Randall County, retrospective testing shows that H5 was detectable in 306

wastewater on Mar 1, 2024 - nearly a week before an unspecified disease was reported 307

in dairy cattle in Texas (Mar 7) and several weeks before the causative agent was 308

identified as H5N1 (Mar 25). Understanding and describing industry inputs into 309

municipal wastewater, especially those that may be associated with contributions from 310

animals, is critical both to identifying anomalies in influenza data from wastewater that 311

do not relate to human disease, and identifying cases when wastewater can provide 312

important, early warning data on outbreaks with zoonotic potential. Future work should 313

further explore the possible contributions of animal shedding to municipal wastewater 314

systems, and seek to sequence influenza A in wastewater to support genomic 315

surveillance. 316
